architectural_implications.before: Plan inference capacity from model throughput/latency benchmarks at batch size 1.
architectural_implications.consequence: Long-horizon agent sessions (long contexts, many tool turns) become the dominant cost driver; context compaction and session lifetime become architectural concerns, not prompt hygiene.
architectural_implications.observation: Serving capacity for agentic workloads is bounded by KV cache growth per concurrent session, not by raw compute.

architectural_implications.after: Harness is a cost/throughput component with an owned-infrastructure price tag, evaluated on tokens-per-resolved-task and GPU wall-time.
architectural_implications.before: Harness is a developer-tooling choice, evaluated on task success and ergonomics.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harness selection, prompt scaffolding, and tool-call verbosity move into platform/ops ownership with continuous benchmarking, and may be routed per workload like models are.
architectural_implications.observation: Harness token efficiency becomes an infrastructure-level cost variable under ownership.

architectural_implications.after: Pick model+hardware pairs as a unit, benchmarked on resolve rate per dollar at target concurrency.
architectural_implications.before: Pick the best model, then pick hardware that can run it.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires an internal benchmarking rig and periodic re-evaluation as new open-weight models appear; the decision surface is combinatorial rather than one-dimensional.
architectural_implications.observation: Model selection and hardware topology become a joint design decision.

connections.relationship: Long tool-use sessions inflate context and therefore KV cache, directly reducing sessions-per-node and raising cost per resolved task.

Viability of owned infrastructure depends on keeping the cluster saturated, making request scheduling and multiplexing an economic lever rather than a latency optimization.
Model routing at stage 2 and infrastructure ownership at stage 4 both require the same per-model cost/quality measurements to steer traffic.
If different model sizes fit different GPU topologies, routing becomes a hardware-placement problem (which node class runs which model) as well as a quality-per-cost problem.

evidence_quotes.text: Concurrency becomes a major bottleneck due to GPU memory limitations imposed by model parameter size and users' KV cache.
Larger models like Kimi K3 dropped to 4 comfortable concurrent users on 8x B300 with 3x higher latency than baseline.

core_insights.generalization: For any long-context agentic workload, memory-per-session (KV cache) rather than FLOPs is the binding constraint on serving density; model size and context length trade directly against tenant count.
core_insights.insight: When self-hosting, concurrency capacity is bounded by GPU memory budget = model weights + per-session KV cache, so 'comfortable concurrency' collapses for large models even on top-end hardware. Kimi K3 fell to ~4 concurrent users on 8x B300 with 3x latency vs baseline.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Capacity planning for self-hosted inference cannot be done from throughput benchmarks or model accuracy alone; the economically relevant number is how many concurrent long-horizon agent sessions fit in HBM after weights, which determines cost per session and SLA.

evidence_quotes.text: Harnesses do not significantly impact resolve rate for API usage, but dramatically impact token consumption and GPU wall-time when managing your own infrastructure.
Codex generated half the tokens of Claude Code and Pi for GLM-5.2-Flash, halving GPU wall-time and infrastructure cost.

core_insights.generalization: When you own the inference layer, any component that controls token generation volume (harness, prompting, tool-call verbosity, context management) is a cost-multiplier with the same leverage as hardware selection.
core_insights.insight: Coding harness choice is a first-order cost variable only under self-hosting: harnesses produce similar resolve rates but wildly different token counts, and token count maps directly to GPU wall-time. Codex generated half the tokens of Claude Code and Pi on GLM-5.2-Flash, halving infrastructure cost.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Under API pricing, token inefficiency is a linear, visible line item; under ownership it becomes a roughly 2x multiplier on GPU capital/rental cost, which makes harness selection and harness token-efficiency benchmarking an ops-layer responsibility rather than a developer preference.

evidence_quotes.text: Lower-tier hardware systems require ~89% GPU utilization to make buying/renting viable, which is nearly infeasible.

core_insights.generalization: Owning compute only pays off above a utilization threshold; below that, the fixed cost of idle silicon dominates and managed/API pricing is rational regardless of per-token markup.
core_insights.insight: Buy-vs-rent-vs-API economics have a hard utilization cliff: lower-tier self-hosted hardware needs ~89% sustained GPU utilization to beat alternatives, which is nearly unreachable, while GLM-class workloads reach roughly 25% savings over API when rented or owned.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The decision hinges on achieved utilization, not sticker price of hardware or tokens — meaning the break-even question is really 'can we keep this cluster saturated with agent traffic', which is an operational scheduling problem.

evidence_quotes.text: Kimi K3 achieved 86.4% resolve rate on 8x B300; Qwen and DeepSeek achieved ~35-39% on 1x H200.

core_insights.generalization: Benchmarks that report only task success hide the cost dimension; model comparisons should be reported as success-per-hardware-dollar-and-concurrency to be decision-useful.
core_insights.insight: Model accuracy gains cascade non-linearly into hardware requirements: Kimi K3 hit 86.4% resolve rate on 8x B300 versus ~35-39% for Qwen/DeepSeek on 1x H200, so a marginal capability improvement changes the machine class and therefore the cost curve.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Model selection and hardware SKU selection cannot be decoupled; choosing a stronger model may silently require an 8x topology, invalidating a capacity plan built around single-GPU nodes.

evidence_quotes.text: Harnesses do not significantly impact resolve rate for API usage, but dramatically impact token consumption and GPU wall-time when managing your own infrastructure.

core_insights.generalization: For agent evaluation, report the cost vector (tokens, wall-time, concurrency footprint) alongside the quality vector; a single scalar quality metric systematically mis-ranks configurations under ownership economics.
core_insights.insight: Resolve-rate is an insufficient evaluation signal: harnesses that are indistinguishable on task success differ by 2x in token consumption, so evaluation harnesses for agent systems should log tokens and wall-time, not just pass/fail.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Teams using resolve rate alone will select harnesses/models that appear equal in quality but are 2x more expensive to operate at scale — an invisible regression until the GPU bill arrives.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Steven Latré
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Benchmarking the full stack of AI systems from silicon to harness, comparing API vs. on-premise infrastructure costs and trade-offs.
  • Purpose: To quantify the cost, accuracy, concurrency, and hardware trade-offs of moving from closed APIs to self-hosted infrastructure for agentic AI tasks. Steven Latré from imec discusses the transition from API-based token consumption to owning and operating your own AI infrastructure, presenting a comprehensive benchmarking study across thousands of runs evaluating models, coding harnesses, and hardware configurations for long-horizon coding tasks.

Topic Map

Introduction to imec and AI Evolution

  • Explanation: Introduction of imec as a leading semiconductor R&D institute and its expansion from silicon up to system workloads and agentic AI flows.
  • Key claims:
    • imec runs the most advanced R&D cleanrooms in the world and invents core transistor technologies.
    • AI maturity moved from wanting the latest frontier models regardless of cost towards subscription pricing, token-based pricing, and model routing.
  • Examples:
    • Model routing to find the best model for task complexity.
  • Terminology:
    • imec
    • model routing
    • frontier models
    • token-based pricing
  • Why it matters: Establishes credibility in bridging semiconductor hardware and AI application workloads.

The Shift in Deployment Stages

  • Explanation: Evolution of deployment from bootstrapping with closed APIs to scaling, integration, and optimization via owning infrastructure.
  • Key claims:
    • Four phases of deployment: 1) bootstrapping (closed API, single model), 2) scaling (model routing), 3) integration (leasing infra), 4) optimization (owning infra).
    • As token consumption grows rapidly, organizations need control over their own stack for predictability, regulation, and security.
  • Examples:
    • Moving from closed APIs to cost optimization, then to leasing, and finally owning infrastructure.
  • Terminology:
    • bootstrapping
    • model routing
    • leasing infrastructure
    • total cost of ownership
  • Why it matters: Highlights why larger token deployments necessitate owning infrastructure.

Benchmarking Setup: SWE-bench PRO

  • Explanation: Methodology for comparing API vs. infrastructure costs using 64 long-horizon coding tasks across various coding harnesses, models, and GPU architectures.
  • Key claims:
    • Evaluated 64 long-horizon coding tasks from SWE-bench PRO.
    • Tested coding harnesses (Codex, Pi, Claude Code) paired with diverse models (Opus 4.8, Qwen 3.6, DeepSeek V4, GLM 5.2, Kimi K3) on hardware ranging from 1x H200 to 8x B300.
  • Examples:
    • Testing Codex, Pi, and Claude Code harnesses with Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi models.
  • Terminology:
    • SWE-bench PRO
    • coding harness
    • resolve rate
    • latency
    • TCO
  • Why it matters: Provides empirical data on the non-linear relationship between models, harnesses, and hardware.

Results: Models, Hardware Costs, and Concurrency

  • Explanation: Analysis of resolve rates, hardware costs, and concurrency bottlenecks when running open-weight models locally.
  • Key claims:
    • Different models with different hardware costs show non-linear cost-performance scaling.
    • Concurrency becomes a major bottleneck due to GPU memory limitations imposed by model parameter size and users' KV cache.
    • Larger models suffer severe drop-offs in comfortable concurrency even on powerful hardware like 8x B300.
  • Examples:
    • Kimi K3 achieved 86.4% resolve rate on 8x B300; Qwen and DeepSeek achieved ~35-39% on 1x H200.
  • Terminology:
    • KV cache
    • concurrency
    • resolve rate
    • GPU memory
    • throughput
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that concurrency and hardware constraints are critical factors beyond raw model accuracy.

API vs. Rent vs. Buy Analysis

  • Explanation: Total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis comparing API usage against renting and buying infrastructure.
  • Key claims:
    • Lower-tier hardware systems require ~89% GPU utilization to make buying/renting viable, which is nearly infeasible.
    • For GLM-class applications, moving from API to rented/owned infrastructure achieves ~25% cost savings.
    • Harnesses do not significantly impact resolve rate for API usage, but dramatically impact token consumption and GPU wall-time when managing your own infrastructure.
  • Examples:
    • GLM-5.2 applications achieving 25% cost savings compared to API.
  • Terminology:
    • total cost of ownership
    • GPU utilization
    • sweet spot
    • token consumption
  • Why it matters: Provides a practical framework for deciding whether to use APIs, rent GPUs, or buy infrastructure.

Key Points

The API-to-Infrastructure decision is non-linear

  • Explanation: Moving from APIs to self-hosted infrastructure involves complex trade-offs between model size, hardware architecture, and token consumption.
  • Evidence: Benchmarking data across 1,000+ runs shows non-linear cost and performance curves.
  • Practical implication: Engineers cannot simply swap APIs for self-hosted models without re-evaluating their entire infrastructure stack.

Concurrency and KV cache are major bottlenecks

  • Explanation: As user concurrency increases, GPU memory must accommodate both model parameters and growing KV caches.
  • Evidence: Larger models like Kimi K3 dropped to 4 comfortable concurrent users on 8x B300 with 3x higher latency than baseline.
  • Practical implication: Concurrency limits can severely degrade the economic viability of self-hosting large models.

Harness choice impacts GPU wall-time and token consumption

  • Explanation: Different coding harnesses generate vastly different numbers of tokens for the same task performance.
  • Evidence: Codex generated half the tokens of Claude Code and Pi for GLM-5.2-Flash, halving GPU wall-time and infrastructure cost.
  • Practical implication: Choosing the wrong harness when managing your own infrastructure can double your GPU bill.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Deployment Stack Optimization Framework

  • How it works: A four-phase maturity model moving from closed APIs to full infrastructure ownership.
  • Components:
      1. Bootstrapping (Closed API - single model)
      1. Scaling (Model routing)
      1. Integration (Leasing infra)
      1. Optimisation (Owning infra)
  • When to use: When scaling AI token consumption and evaluating cost-efficiency vs. operational control.

Examples & Case Studies

Benchmarking Kimi K3 vs. Qwen 3.6 on SWE-bench PRO tasks across different GPU counts.

  • Illustrates: Different models require vastly different hardware architectures and incur non-linear cost increases.
  • Lesson: Selecting a slightly better or worse model has massive downstream impacts on hardware requirements and rental costs.

Comparing Codex, Claude Code, and Pi harnesses using GLM-5.2-Flash.

  • Illustrates: Harnesses affect token consumption and GPU wall-time despite achieving similar application resolve rates.
  • Lesson: Pairing the wrong harness with your own infrastructure can double your GPU costs.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Evaluate your token consumption growth before deciding to move off APIs.
    • Account for KV cache and concurrency limits when sizing GPU memory for self-hosted models.
  • Strategic:
    • 25%+ cost savings are achievable by moving to self-hosted infra for specific model classes (like GLM) if managed carefully.
    • Software and hardware worlds need closer integration through alliances like the aistack alliance.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do quantization and speculative decoding impact self-hosted TCO?
    • What is the optimal GPU-to-CPU balance for specific agentic AI workloads?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Lower-tier hardware systems require 89% GPU utilization to make renting/buying viable. (economic_claim)
  • Kimi K3 achieved an 86.4% resolve rate on SWE-bench PRO using 8x B300. (benchmark_claim)

Notable Quotes

"For the same task performance, what costs will we have? (token-based to total cost of ownership)" (at 8:36) "Suddenly the design space blows up." (at 5:41) "The API to infra decision is fast from linear." (at 27:09)

Compressed Summary

  • Benchmarking API vs. self-hosted infrastructure across 64 SWE-bench PRO tasks.
  • Concurrency and KV cache scaling present major bottlenecks for self-hosted large models.
  • Harness choice dramatically affects token consumption and GPU wall-time.
  • Careful management enables 25%+ cost savings when transitioning from APIs to self-hosted infra.
  • Keywords: benchmarking, infrastructure, concurrency, kv-cache, tco
  • Core insight: Moving from APIs to self-hosted AI infrastructure offers significant cost savings (25%+), but introduces complex trade-offs in hardware scaling, concurrency limits, and token efficiency across coding harnesses.

### Results: Models, Hardware Costs, and Concurrency
- **Explanation**: Analysis of resolve rates, hardware costs, and concurrency bottlenecks when running open-weight models locally.
- **Key claims**:
  - Different models with different hardware costs show non-linear cost-performance scaling.
  - Concurrency becomes a major bottleneck due to GPU memory limitations imposed by model parameter size and users' KV cache.
  - Larger models suffer severe drop-offs in comfortable concurrency even on powerful hardware like 8x B300.
- **Examples**:
  - Kimi K3 achieved 86.4% resolve rate on 8x B300; Qwen and DeepSeek achieved ~35-39% on 1x H200.

### API vs. Rent vs. Buy Analysis
- **Explanation**: Total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis comparing API usage against renting and buying infrastructure.
- **Key claims**:
  - Lower-tier hardware systems require ~89% GPU utilization to make buying/renting viable, which is nearly infeasible.
  - For GLM-class applications, moving from API to rented/owned infrastructure achieves ~25% cost savings.
  - Harnesses do not significantly impact resolve rate for API usage, but dramatically impact token consumption and GPU wall-time when managing your own infrastructure.
- **Examples**:

- **Why it matters**: Provides a practical framework for deciding whether to use APIs, rent GPUs, or buy infrastructure.
## Key Points
### The API-to-Infrastructure decision is non-linear
- **Explanation**: Moving from APIs to self-hosted infrastructure involves complex trade-offs between model size, hardware architecture, and token consumption.
- **Evidence**: Benchmarking data across 1,000+ runs shows non-linear cost and performance curves.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers cannot simply swap APIs for self-hosted models without re-evaluating their entire infrastructure stack.
### Concurrency and KV cache are major bottlenecks
- **Explanation**: As user concurrency increases, GPU memory must accommodate both model parameters and growing KV caches.
- **Evidence**: Larger models like Kimi K3 dropped to 4 comfortable concurrent users on 8x B300 with 3x higher latency than baseline.
- **Practical implication**: Concurrency limits can severely degrade the economic viability of self-hosting large models.
### Harness choice impacts GPU wall-time and token consumption
- **Explanation**: Different coding harnesses generate vastly different numbers of tokens for the same task performance.
- **Evidence**: Codex generated half the tokens of Claude Code and Pi for GLM-5.2-Flash, halving GPU wall-time and infrastructure cost.
- **Practical implication**: Choosing the wrong harness when managing your own infrastructure can double your GPU bill.
